What complicates it is the 27% strikeout rate, because that translates to 29.5% against big-league pitching, and a hit tool that grades 55 can carry a 27% K-rate in the minors long before it can carry one against advanced arms. If the contact holds, Walton profiles as a low-end everyday regular with speed-and-power upside; if pitchers find the hole, what's left is a bench bat with real pop.

830336_pitcher.text: The 2.1 ERA across A+ & A is the loud number, but what makes it worth taking seriously is the shape behind it: 87 strikeouts in 64.3 innings with only 19 walks, a 0.9 WHIP, a K-BB% of 27 that ranks at the 98th percentile in his pool. Strip that down to what it translates to at the MLB level and it deflates quickly — the strikeout rate comes out to 8.4 per nine, essentially matching what an average major-league arm produces, and the walk rate lands in the same neighborhood, so the margins that look dominant in A-ball basically become a league-average pitcher. That's the whole profile: the stuff plays up in the lower minors, and if it doesn't add a genuine swing-and-miss weapon as he climbs, the floor is a depth arm with no real ceiling to argue over.

830402_pitcher.text: The control is the whole argument. Across A+ & A, Kendry Chourio has walked 17 batters in 90.7 innings, a 1.7 BB/9 that translates to a 2.5 MLB-equivalent against a pool where 3.2 is ordinary. The WHIP sits at 0.9, and the ERA at 2.5, both gaudy enough to explain why an 18-year-old is drawing attention, but the strikeout rate is the honest complication: his 9.0 K/9 translates to a 7.1 MLB-equivalent, well below the 8.6 that qualifies as baseline. If the command holds as he climbs and the stuff develops enough to push the swing-and-miss rate toward that baseline, there's a back-end starter here; if the strikeouts don't grow, the command alone lands him as a depth arm.

832562_pitcher.text: The K-BB% is the loudest thing in this profile: 24% across A+ & A, which translates to a 14.1% MLB-equivalent, right at the middle of the big-league pack. That's a lefty who commands the zone well enough that the strikeout volume, 143 across 106.6 innings, doesn't feel like a walk-rate trade-off. The translated BB/9 of 3.6 sits a tick higher than his translated K/9 of 8.7 would prefer, so the command isn't spotless, but the overall shape says a guy who misses bats without missing the zone at an alarming rate. The ceiling here is a depth arm, and the floor is the same; if the strikeout rate flattens against better hitters without the walk rate tightening, there isn't a deeper profile underneath to fall back on.

834962_hitter.text: Seventeen home runs across AA & A+ in 370 plate appearances, with 48 walks against 79 strikeouts, is a bat-first first baseman profile that carries real weight at Double-A. The .218 ISO translates to .156 against MLB pitching, and the translated 10.2% walk rate clears the MLB average of 8.5%, so the approach adds something even after the level discount. A 13% walk rate and .378 OBP suggest someone who can put a lineup together rather than just feast on minor-league arms. If the contact, 21% strikeouts and .266 average, survives the jump, DePino is a low-end everyday regular at first; if it doesn't, the power alone leaves a useful bench bat.

834978_pitcher.text: The minor-league numbers are tidy — 3.4 ERA and a 1.2 WHIP across AA & A+, with 124 strikeouts in 100.3 innings, but the translation is where the profile gets honest. Converted to MLB context, his K/9 lands right at league average and his walk rate comes in above it, leaving a K-BB% of 13.4% against the MLB average of 13.5%. Everything hinges on whether the stuff plays up enough at the highest levels to keep that strikeout rate from slipping further, because if it does, the floor and the ceiling collapse into the same thing: a depth arm who fits the 40-man in a pinch but doesn't hold a rotation spot.
